mcqs.question: What two conditions does the answer skeleton require before denormalizing a data model?
options: The team must have a spare engineer available, and the change must ship before the next release
Reads must vastly outnumber writes with a measurably too-high join cost, and you must explicitly accept the update-anomaly risk
The database must support foreign keys, and the table must have fewer than ten columns
The data must be accessed from more than one microservice at the same time
mcqs.explanation: Denormalization is justified by a real read/write imbalance plus a measured join cost, paired with an explicit acceptance of the staleness or update-fan-out risk it creates. Team availability, foreign-key support, column count, and multi-service access aren't part of this justification.

mcqs.question: What happens to previously-posted comments when a user renames themselves, under the embedded-display-name design?
options: The comments continue showing the old name until something explicitly propagates the update to each embedded copy
The comments automatically re-fetch the new name the next time they're rendered
The comments become permanently unreadable until the user renames themselves back
The database automatically detects the rename and cascades it to all embedded copies instantly
mcqs.explanation: Since the name was copied at write time, embedded copies stay stale until an explicit process updates them — this is the expected trade-off of denormalization, not a bug. There's no automatic re-fetch or cascade in this design, and the comments remain fully readable, just with outdated names.

mcqs.question: What is the trade-off to name explicitly when denormalizing a relationship?
options: It permanently prevents the underlying source-of-truth table from ever being updated again
It has no real cost once the initial embedding is implemented correctly
It buys read speed at the cost of update fan-out — one write becomes many, or you accept staleness instead
It only applies to relational databases and has no equivalent concept in NoSQL systems
mcqs.explanation: Denormalization trades read speed for either propagating updates to every duplicated copy or accepting that they'll drift stale — a real, ongoing cost either way. It doesn't freeze the source table, isn't free once implemented, and the concept applies at least as much in NoSQL document models as relational ones.

mcqs.question: Why is denormalizing on the general belief that "joins are slower than no joins" considered a pitfall?
options: It accepts a real ongoing cost — update anomalies and duplication — against a performance problem that hasn't been shown to actually exist for this query
Joins are actually faster than denormalized reads in every database system
Denormalization is only a valid technique for tables with a single column
It's technically impossible to denormalize a relationship without first sharding the database
mcqs.explanation: The pitfall is paying denormalization's real cost — duplication and potential staleness — for a performance problem that was never actually measured or confirmed. Joins aren't universally faster or slower than denormalized reads, denormalization isn't limited to single-column tables, and it has no sharding prerequisite.
